newsitem.title: IRAQ: Pro-Baghdad Iraqi Kurds stalled in dam attack.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Baghdad Iraqi Kurds stalled in dam attack.

text.p: Rival Kurdish forces were engaged in fierce fighting on Sunday for control of northern Iraq's strategic Dukan Dam ahead of U.S. peace talks to end the fighting.
Witnesses said Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) forces stalled an advance by their Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) rivals who had pushed to within five km (three miles) of the dam.

Massoud Barzani's KDP, which received Iraqi military backing during earlier fighting in August, were attempting to take the dam in a push to recapture their rival's stronghold Sulaimaniya, the mountainous region's biggest city.

A KDP Toyota landcruiser with a machinegun mounted on it lay burned and mangled by the side of a road near the frontline, hit by what the group said was a PUK rocket-propelled grenade in close combat.
The charred bodies of KDP fighters were inside the vehicle. The corpses of five other people were strewn on the roadside nearby, apparently victims of another PUK attack.
Barzani's militia could not move a 155-mm artillery gun, which they had used earlier in the day, closer to the dam because of rugged terrain, KDP fighters said.
The defending PUK forces fired lighter artillery rounds.
The dam lies on a main road to the city from territory held by Barzani to the west and north.
"We'll try to reach Dukan Dam today," leading KDP commander Roj Nuri Shuwayis had told Reuters earlier. He said there were other clashes in nearby mountains.
"The big clashes are in the mountains," he said.
The United States has called on both sides to end the fighting, which has weakened U.S. influence in north Iraq and threatened to draw in Iran and Iraq.

Robert Pelletreau, U.S. assistant secretary of state for near eastern affairs, was due in Ankara later on Sunday to meet with Barzani in southeast Turkey. The envoy is to meet PUK leader Jalal Talabani in Turkey later.
"Tomorrow morning he is going to the southeast to meet Barzani," a Turkish foreign ministry official in Ankara said.
The Kurds broke from Baghdad at the end of the 1991 Gulf War and set up a power-sharing parliament that has since collapsed under the weight of the Kurdish feud.

President Saddam Hussein had been kept out of the Kurdish region by U.S.-led air patrols over northern Iraq until Barzani joined with Baghdad's forces to take the city of Arbil -- seat of the former parliament -- on August 31.
Washington last month evacuated more than 2,000 Kurds who had worked for U.S. military, aid and intelligence programmes in northern Iraq and feared Saddam's return to the region.
Around 700 other Iraqi Kurds linked to U.S.-affiliated organisations took refuge in Turkey overnight, Turkish border officials said on Sunday.
Turkish customs officers and two U.S. officials questioned them on their arrival, witnesses said.
Talabani's group said in a statement that Iraqi forces were taking part in the KDP's latest drive but there was no clear sign on the ground of Iraqi government intervention.
Barzani has denied receiving further aid from Baghdad and has in turn accused Talabani of fighting alongside Iranian forces in northern Iraq, a charge Talabani and Tehran deny.
